means: A hypothetical AI that could learn and do almost any mental task a person can, rather than one narrow job.
A doorway that lets one program ask another for something. Apps use an AI company's API to send it text and get answers back.
An AI trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are LLMs.
OpenAI's family of language models. "Generative" = it writes text, "pre-trained" = it first learned from lots of text, "transformer" = its design.
Getting computers to learn patterns from examples instead of being given step-by-step rules.
Getting computers to learn patterns from examples instead of being given step-by-step rules.
A chip with thousands of small cores that do many simple maths jobs at the same time. Built for video games, now the main engine of AI.
The general-purpose 'brain' chip of a computer. Very flexible, but does only a handful of things at once.
Google's own chip designed just for AI maths.
A small AI chip built into phones and laptops to run AI features without the cloud.
A chip designed to do one job extremely well, instead of being general purpose.
NVIDIA's software toolkit for programming its GPUs. Most AI code is built on it, which helps keep people buying NVIDIA.
The American company that makes most of the GPUs used to train and run AI.
The Taiwanese company that physically manufactures most of the world's advanced chips, including NVIDIA's and Apple's.
A Dutch company — the only maker of the EUV machines needed to print the most advanced chips.
Very short-wavelength light used to print the tiniest chip patterns. Shorter light = finer lines, like a sharper pencil.
A powerful NVIDIA GPU (launched 2022) that became the workhorse for training AI models. Costs about as much as a car.
A computer's fast short-term memory. It holds what is being worked on right now and forgets it when the power goes off.
The common, cheap kind of RAM used as main memory in computers and GPUs.
Very fast, very expensive memory built right onto the chip. Tiny in size but quick to reach.
Stacks of memory chips placed right next to a GPU so data can flow to it extremely fast.
Long-term storage with no moving parts. Slower than RAM but keeps data when the power is off.
A fast way of connecting SSD storage to a computer.
A small, fast store of recently used data kept close by so it doesn't need fetching again from somewhere slower.
The smallest, fastest level of cache, right next to each processor core. L2 is a bit bigger and slower.
The smallest piece of information: a single 0 or 1, like a light switch being off or on.
A group of 8 bits. Enough to store one letter of text.
About a million bytes. A typical phone photo is 2–5 MB.
About a billion bytes, or 1,000 MB. A film is a few GB.
About a trillion bytes, or 1,000 GB.
One arithmetic step (like a multiply or add) on a decimal number. Counting FLOPs measures how much computing work was done.
A speed rating for AI chips: how many trillion simple sums they can do each second.
A way to store a decimal number using 32 bits. Precise but uses a lot of memory. FP16, BF16 and FP8 use fewer bits: less precise, faster and smaller.
Storing numbers as whole numbers using just 8 bits — much smaller and faster than decimals, at some loss of precision.
How many bits a computer uses to store each number. More bits = more exact but slower and bigger.
A microscopic on/off switch. A modern chip has billions of them; every calculation is built from these switching.
A material like silicon that can be made to conduct electricity or not. Chips are made from it, so chips are often just called 'semiconductors'.
A thin, dinner-plate-sized disc of pure silicon. Hundreds of chips are printed on each one, then cut apart.
Short for 'fabrication plant': a factory that makes chips. A top-end one costs over $20 billion.
Printing chip patterns by shining light through a stencil onto light-sensitive coating, a bit like developing a photo.
A billion cycles per second. Used for chip clock speeds and radio frequencies (WiFi uses 2.4 and 5 GHz).
A million cycles per second. FM radio is around 100 MHz.
How many times something repeats each second, like how fast a wave goes up and down.
How much data can flow through a connection each second — the width of the pipe.
The delay before something arrives or responds — how long you wait for the first drop, not how wide the pipe is.
Computer systems that do things we'd call smart if a person did them: understanding language, recognising images, making decisions.
In AI, the trained program itself: a giant set of numbers that turns an input (like your question) into an output (an answer).
A model made of layers of simple maths units loosely inspired by brain cells. Each unit multiplies its inputs by numbers, adds them up and passes the result on.
One unit in a neural network: it takes some numbers in, weighs them, adds them up, and passes one number on.
One stage of a neural network. Data passes through layers in order, each transforming it a bit more.
One of the adjustable numbers inside a model. Training tunes them. A big model has billions — think of them as billions of tiny dials.
Another word for a model's parameters: the numbers that say how strongly each input should count.
Showing a model lots of examples and nudging its numbers each time it's wrong, until it gets good at the task.
Using an already-trained model to get an answer. Training = studying; inference = sitting the exam.
A collection of examples used to train or test a model.
A chunk of text a model reads — usually a word or part of a word. 'Unbelievable' might be 3 tokens: un + believ + able. ~1 token ≈ ¾ of a word.
The tool that chops text into tokens before the model sees it.
The full list of tokens a model knows, often 50,000–200,000 of them.
A list of numbers that represents a token or idea. Similar meanings get similar lists, so 'cat' sits near 'kitten'.
Just a list of numbers, like [0.2, -1.3, 0.8]. Can be pictured as an arrow pointing somewhere in space.
A grid of numbers (rows and columns). Neural networks are mostly lots of matrices multiplied together.
A general name for a block of numbers: a list, a grid, or a stack of grids.
Multiply two lists of numbers pair by pair and add the results. A big result means the two lists 'point the same way' — they're similar.
The neural network design behind modern chatbots (2017). Its trick, attention, lets every word look at every other word.
The step where each token looks at the other tokens and decides which ones matter for understanding it — like 'it' looking back to find what 'it' refers to.
How much text a model can look at at once — its working memory, measured in tokens.
A score for how wrong the model is. Training tries to push loss down. Lower = better predictions.
For each of the model's numbers, which direction to nudge it (and how hard) to make the loss smaller. Like feeling which way is downhill in fog.
The training recipe: work out the downhill direction (the gradient), take a small step that way, repeat millions of times.
The method for working out every parameter's gradient: start from the error at the output and pass the blame backwards through the layers.
How big a step training takes each update. Too big and it overshoots; too small and it takes forever.
The algorithm that decides exactly how to update the parameters using the gradients. Adam is the most popular one.
The most common optimizer. It keeps a running average of recent gradients so each parameter gets its own sensible step size.
Gradient descent using small random batches of examples instead of the whole dataset each step.
One full pass through the whole training dataset.
A saved snapshot of a model's numbers partway through training, so you can resume or roll back.
When a model memorises its training examples instead of learning the general pattern, so it does badly on anything new.
The number a neuron outputs after doing its sum. Also short for the 'activation function' that bends that number.
A simple bend applied to each neuron's output (e.g. 'turn negatives into zero'). Without it, stacking layers would add nothing new.
The most common activation function: keep positive numbers, turn negative numbers into 0.
An S-shaped function that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1.
The raw score a model gives each possible next token before they are turned into probabilities.
A formula that turns a list of raw scores into probabilities that add up to 100%. Bigger scores get bigger shares.
A dial for how random a model's word choices are. Low = safe and predictable; high = more surprising.
The plainest kind of neural network: layers of neurons, each connected to all of the next. Transformers contain MLP blocks.
A network that scans an image with small sliding filters to spot edges, then shapes, then objects. Dominated image AI before transformers.
An older design that reads text one word at a time, carrying a memory forward. Slow to train and forgetful over long text.
Two networks competing: one makes fake images, the other tries to spot fakes. Both improve. Popular for images before diffusion models.
A way to generate images: start from pure noise and remove it step by step until a picture appears.
A 2018 Google model that reads text in both directions to understand it. Great for search and classification, not for writing.
A 2021 OpenAI model that learned to match images with their captions, putting both into the same 'meaning space'.
A model split into many 'expert' sub-networks where only a few are used for each token. Lots of knowledge, less computing per word.
In 'KV cache': the saved attention notes for earlier tokens, kept so the model doesn't redo work for every new word.
Memory where a model stores its notes about earlier tokens so it doesn't recompute them for each new word it writes.
Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits (e.g. 8 instead of 16). Smaller and faster, with a little loss of accuracy.
Training a small 'student' model to copy a big 'teacher' model's answers, getting much of its skill cheaply.
Taking an already-trained model and training it a bit more on a smaller, specific dataset to specialise it.
The first, giant phase of training: the model reads trillions of tokens of text and learns to predict the next one.
Everything done after pretraining to turn a raw text-predictor into a helpful, safe assistant.
A model straight out of pretraining. It continues text but doesn't yet behave like a helpful assistant.
Learning where the answers come from the data itself — e.g. hide the next word and guess it — so no human has to label anything.
A standard test used to compare models, like an exam every model sits.
A popular benchmark of ~16,000 multiple-choice questions across 57 school and university subjects.
Learning by trial and error: try something, get a reward or penalty, do more of what got rewarded.
Learning by trial and error: try something, get a reward or penalty, do more of what got rewarded.
A model trained to score answers the way humans would, used to guide another model's training.
People compare pairs of answers; a model learns their preferences; the chatbot is then trained to produce answers people prefer.
Like RLHF, but an AI model does the judging instead of people.
A simpler alternative to RLHF that trains directly on 'answer A is better than B' pairs, with no separate reward model.
A standard reinforcement-learning algorithm that improves a model in small, careful steps so it doesn't change too wildly.
An RL method (used by DeepSeek) that scores a group of answers to the same question and rewards the better-than-average ones.
A measure of how different two probability patterns are. Used as a leash to stop a model drifting too far from its original behaviour.
Before answering, the AI searches a set of documents and pastes the relevant bits into its prompt, so it answers from real sources.
An open standard (from Anthropic) for plugging AI assistants into tools and data, like a USB port for AI apps.
An AI that doesn't just answer but takes actions in steps — searching, clicking, running code — to finish a goal.
The text you give a model: your question plus any instructions or examples.
When an AI confidently states something false or made-up.
A model whose trained numbers are published, so anyone can download and run it themselves.
Computing power — how many calculations you can afford. In AI it usually means GPU-hours.
A pattern showing a model gets predictably better as you add more data, parameters and compute.
A relationship where each 10× increase in one thing gives the same fixed improvement in another. Plotted on log scales it's a straight line.
A chart where both axes jump by multiples of 10 (1, 10, 100, 1000…) instead of evenly. Power laws look straight on it.
A 2022 DeepMind study and model showing that, for a fixed budget, you should train on about 20 tokens of text per parameter.
A free, public archive of billions of web pages, used as a main source of AI training text.
Training data made by AI models rather than written by people.
What fraction of a GPU's top theoretical speed a training run actually uses. Around 40% is good.
Meta's family of open-weight language models.
A Chinese AI lab known for strong, cheap open-weight models such as DeepSeek-V3 and R1.
A puzzle benchmark of coloured-grid patterns that are easy for people but hard for AI. Used to test general reasoning.
As in SWE-bench: a benchmark of real coding bugs from GitHub that a model has to fix.
A benchmark of ~8,500 grade-school maths word problems.
A non-profit that measures how long and complex the tasks AI agents can complete on their own are.
An alternative to transformers (e.g. Mamba) that reads text in order with a fixed-size memory, so long inputs stay cheap.
A trick where several attention heads share the same stored notes, shrinking memory use.
A way to train across many GPUs by splitting the model's numbers among them, so no single GPU has to hold everything.
NVIDIA's software for fast data-sharing between GPUs during training.
Total data-centre power ÷ power used by the computers. 1.1 means only 10% extra goes on cooling and other overhead.
A million watts — roughly what 1,000 homes use at once. GW (gigawatt) is 1,000 MW.
A huge amount of energy: a trillion watt-hours. A country like Ireland uses about 30 TWh a year.
A warehouse full of computers, with serious power and cooling. Where AI is trained and run.
Computers you rent over the internet instead of owning.
Software whose code is published for anyone to use, study and change.
A precise set of steps for solving a problem, like a recipe.
How likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain). 0.25 = 25% = 1 in 4.
The full spread of possibilities and how likely each one is.
RL on tasks with checkable answers (maths, code tests), so the reward is simply 'was it right?'.
When a model writes out its reasoning step by step before giving the final answer.
Able to handle more than one kind of input — text plus images, audio or video.
A model that can look at images and talk about them.
Turning written text into spoken audio.
The share of words a speech-recogniser gets wrong. Lower is better.
The molecule that stores the genetic instructions for living things.
A language for asking databases questions, like 'show every customer in London'.
A simple text format for structured data, using { } and lists. Programs use it to swap information.
A web address, like https://example.com.
The secure, encrypted version of the protocol your browser uses to fetch web pages. The padlock icon.
Scrambling data with a secret key so only someone with the right key can read it.
An agreed set of rules for how devices talk to each other, like the etiquette of a phone call.
A small chunk of data sent over a network. Big files are split into many packets and put back together.
The box that directs data between your devices and the internet.
The box that connects your home to your internet provider's line (cable, fibre or phone).
The addressing system of the internet. Every device online gets an IP address so data knows where to go.
The internet's phone book: it turns names like google.com into the number addresses computers use.
The rules that make sure all packets arrive, in order, and resend any that go missing.
The encryption that puts the S (secure) in HTTPS.
How long a message takes to go somewhere and for the reply to come back.
Wireless networking that links your devices to your router using radio waves.
An engineering body that writes technical standards. WiFi's official name is IEEE 802.11.
Splitting one radio channel into many thin sub-channels that carry data side by side, so interference only spoils a few.
Encoding bits by setting a wave's strength and timing to one of many patterns. More patterns = more bits per send.
Using several antennas at once to send multiple data streams through the same air.
'Listen before you talk': a device checks the channel is quiet before sending.
The WiFi security standard that encrypts your traffic. WPA3 is the newer, stronger version.
The original WiFi security from 1999 — now easily broken in minutes.
A piece of metal shaped to send or catch radio waves.
The range of radio frequencies. Governments divide it up and license slices to phone networks, TV, WiFi and so on.
The fourth generation of mobile networks (2010s). Brought fast mobile internet and video.
The fifth generation of mobile networks: faster speeds, lower delay, and room for many more devices.
The technology behind 4G mobile data.
The small chip that proves to the mobile network who you are and which plan you pay for.
Plain text messages over the phone network.
A mast with antennas that talks to phones in a patch of area called a 'cell'.
Satellites that broadcast precise time signals; your phone works out where it is from how long each signal took.
A quantum bit. Unlike a normal bit (0 or 1), it can be in a blend of both until it's measured.
A quantum state that is a blend of possibilities (like 0 and 1) at the same time, until it's measured.
A quantum link between particles so measuring one instantly tells you about the other.
When a fragile quantum state gets disturbed by its surroundings and loses its quantum behaviour — the main enemy of quantum computers.
Today's era of quantum computers: a few hundred to a few thousand error-prone qubits.
A widely used encryption method whose security depends on how hard it is to split huge numbers into their prime factors.
The standard way to scramble data with a secret key, used almost everywhere.
A function that turns any data into a short fingerprint. Change one letter and the fingerprint changes completely.
An old standard that gives each English letter, digit and symbol a number from 0–127.
UTF-8 is the standard way to store text from every language as bytes.
A logic rule: output 1 if exactly one of two inputs is 1. Famous because a single-layer network can't learn it.
The total value of everything a country produces in a year — a measure of the size of its economy.
The EU's strict privacy law about how companies collect and use personal data.
A group of 27 European countries that share many laws and a single market.

full: National Institute of Standards and Technology
means: A US government agency that sets technical standards, including for encryption and AI safety.
The US military's research agency. It funded early internet and AI research.
A classic keyword-search scoring formula: ranks documents by how often your search words appear, weighting rare words more.
A fast way to find the most similar vectors in a huge collection, by hopping through a layered map of neighbours.
A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the ones most similar to a query.
A file format for running quantized language models on ordinary computers.
A standard for attaching tamper-evident 'where this came from' labels to images and videos.
A car powered by a battery and electric motor.
The standard type of transistor inside modern chips.
A chipmaker that competes with Intel for CPUs and with NVIDIA for GPUs.
A long-running US computing company, known for early AI like Deep Blue and Watson and for quantum computers.

full: European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts
means: Europe's main weather-forecasting centre, home of one of the world's best weather models.
A two-yearly competition to predict protein shapes. DeepMind's AlphaFold won it in 2020.
A molecular machine made from a chain of building blocks that folds into a 3D shape; the shape decides its job.
A top US university. The 'MIT license' it wrote lets anyone use software almost freely.
DeepMind's 2013–15 system that learned to play Atari games from screen pixels using reinforcement learning.
DeepSeek-R1: a Chinese open-weight reasoning model released in January 2025 that rivalled OpenAI's best, cheaply.
DeepSeek-V3: a large, cheap-to-train open-weight model from Chinese lab DeepSeek (December 2024).
A big management consultancy, known in AI for studies of how consultants work with chatbots.
NVIDIA's high-end GPU format that plugs straight into a server board for more power and faster links.
An NVIDIA data-centre GPU from 2017, two generations before the H100.
A hard high-school maths competition, used as a benchmark for reasoning models.
A plastic disc storing music or data as microscopic pits read by a laser.
Computers, servers and networks — in a data centre, the actual computing gear as opposed to cooling and power.
An open-source model design that mixes RNN-style memory with transformer-style training.
A 1966 chatbot that imitated a therapist by rephrasing what you typed. People got surprisingly attached to it.
A way of carrying sound on radio by wobbling the wave's frequency. FM radio stations sit around 88–108 MHz.
A rule for distributed databases: during a network split you must choose between Consistency and Availability.
As in QR code: a square barcode a phone camera can read.
Google's 2019 'Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer', which framed every language task as text in, text out.
The core 'multiply two big grids of numbers' operation that AI chips are built to do fast.
NVIDIA's older line of gaming graphics cards. Two GTX 580s trained AlexNet in 2012.
A popular method for quantizing (shrinking) a language model to about 4 bits after training.
Intelligence quotient: a score from standard human intelligence tests.
An image model trained by hiding most of each picture and learning to fill it back in.
DALL·E: OpenAI's image-generation models (2021 onward).
A format that stores music as notes and timings (like sheet music) rather than recorded sound.
The US music-industry trade group.
A large US public university system (Berkeley, Los Angeles, etc.).
The research group behind Chatbot Arena, where people vote between two anonymous chatbots' answers.
Anthropic's safety tiers: higher ASL levels require stricter safeguards for more capable models.
An NVIDIA product pairing two Blackwell GPUs with a Grace CPU. The NVL72 rack links 72 GPUs as one giant machine.
An intergovernmental body that tracks world energy use.
A large Swiss bank whose analysts publish widely quoted estimates.
A way to squash data with many measurements down to the few directions where it varies most.
Meta's own in-house AI chip.
AMD's data-centre AI GPU, a rival to NVIDIA's H100.
Apple's 2017 iPhone chip, the first with a built-in 'Neural Engine' for AI.
Europe's main life-sciences research lab, which hosts the AlphaFold protein database.
A molecule similar to DNA that carries genetic instructions to the cell's protein-making machinery.
A huge record of past global weather from 1940 onward, used to train AI weather models.
A tool for looking inside a model: it splits the model's internal signals into thousands of readable 'features'.
Video at 720 or 1080 lines tall — sharper than old TV, less than 4K.
A WiFi 6 router speed label: the 5400 is the total maximum speed in Mbps across all its bands, which no single device ever gets.
An extension of CAP: even without a network split, databases trade off latency (speed) against consistency.
A newer internet transport protocol (used by HTTP/3) that sets up secure connections faster than TCP plus TLS.
The US space agency.
A major US computer maker from the 1960s to 1990s.
An 'expert system' DEC used in the 1980s to configure VAX computer orders using thousands of hand-written rules.
An Israeli AI lab that makes the Jamba language models.
The calm, murderous computer in the 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey.
A small humanoid robot from Chinese maker Unitree.
A proposed law in a US state senate, e.g. California's SB 1047.
A short fingerprint computed from any data. The same input always gives the same hash; change one letter and it changes completely.
For hashes: two different inputs that happen to produce the same fingerprint.
A measure of unpredictability or randomness. More entropy = harder to guess.
A computer that runs all the time to answer requests from other devices — e.g. sending you a web page.
An organised store of data that programs can search and update quickly.
The science of scrambling and unscrambling information so only the right people can read it.
In encryption, the half of a key pair you share openly. Anyone can use it to lock a message that only your private key can open.
The secret half of a key pair. It unlocks messages locked with your public key, and proves your identity.
The small raised number saying how many times to multiply: 2⁵ = 2×2×2×2×2 = 32.
How spread out a set of numbers is from their average. Bigger variance = more scattered.
A consistent lean in one direction — in data or people — that skews results away from the truth.
In statistics: fitting a line or curve to data to predict one thing from another. 'Regression to the mean' is the tendency for extreme results to be followed by more ordinary ones.
When two things tend to rise and fall together. It doesn't prove one causes the other.
In a study, the chance of seeing results at least this extreme if there were really no effect. Small p-values (like under 0.05) are called 'significant'.
Bayes' rule: how to update a belief when new evidence arrives, weighing how likely the evidence is if the belief is true versus false.
The average result you'd get if you repeated something many times: each outcome × its chance, added up.
Counting with only two digits, 0 and 1. Computers store everything this way.
In networks: when a link breaks and computers split into groups that can't reach each other.
The distance from one peak of a wave to the next. Shorter wavelength = higher frequency.
A program that translates code people write into instructions a computer's chip can run.
A fund you can buy like a share that holds many investments at once, often a whole stock index.
A fund that simply buys everything in a market index (like the S&P 500), so you own a slice of all of it at low cost.
Prices rising over time, so the same money buys less.
Earning interest on your interest, so growth snowballs over time.
The standard plug and cable for connecting devices like keyboards, drives and phone chargers.
